publications.title: Implementasi Sistem Informasi Analisis Laboratorium Berbasis Web pada PT Multi Nitrotama Kimia Karawang
publications.abstract: Quality control in the chemical industry requires accurate and timely recording of process parameters. At PT Multi Nitrotama Kimia, laboratory results from three production plants—the Ammonium Nitrate Plant, Nitric Acid Plant, and Utility Plant—were recorded on paper logsheets and compiled in separate spreadsheets. This practice increased transcription errors, delayed report circulation, and provided no automatic warnings for parameters exceeding specified limits. This study aims to develop ANLAB, a web-based Laboratory Analysis Information System. The system was developed using the Waterfall model, PHP, CodeIgniter 3, and MySQL. Data were collected through observations, interviews with analysts, Distributed Control System (DCS) operators and supervisors, and document reviews. ANLAB features digital forms that classify results as normal, above, or below limits; a three-tier approval workflow; additional check requests; plant shutdown tagging; role-based access control; and PDF and Excel report exports. Black box testing involving 27 scenarios confirmed that all tested functions produced the expected results. However, testing focused exclusively on functionality; time savings, error reduction, and paperless performance were not measured. Future evaluations should assess these indicators using system timestamps. The findings indicate that ANLAB provides a structured and traceable digital workflow for laboratory data management in chemical plant operations

publications.title: Real Health Economics Ontology (RHEO)
publications.abstract: The Real Health Economics Ontology (RHEO) describes the real things that health economics works with, such as patients, households, care settings, resources, payments and costs, and the records made about them. It also describes the evidence built from these records, from estimates and assumptions to model parameters and results, so that a model result can be traced back to its sources. RHEO is written in the Web Ontology Language (OWL) and is aligned to the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) 2020. Its relationships to the concepts of the Health Economics Ontology (HEO) are published as a separate mapping file. This is an alpha release for review, and terms may still change before version 1.0.

publications.title: Media and Creative Industries and Artificial Intelligence: Heavy Early Use, Unsettled Rights, and an Audience Moving Towards Chatbots
publications.abstract: Purpose. Media and creative work produce text, images, sound and video, which are the outputs that generative AI makes. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in the media and creative industries in 2026 and where they may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review combining the share of the media research literature that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), Eurostat's survey of AI use in EU enterprises in publishing, film, television, music and broadcasting (2021–2025), an online experiment on creativity and AI, the Reuters Institute's 2026 survey of news audiences, a streaming company's figures on AI music uploads, labour agreements in the film industry, and the copyright and transparency rules in the United States and the EU. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of media works that mention AI rose from 0.9% in 2018 to 4.9% in 2025, 5.5 times as much, and language-model works from 70 to 1,681. In the EU, 56.2% of enterprises in publishing, film, television, music and broadcasting used AI in 2025, up from 18.0% in 2021 and the second-highest share after software among the twelve sectors with Eurostat data, nearly three times the 19.9% for all enterprises. Output is changing faster than the rules. A streaming company reported that fully AI-generated tracks rose from about 10% of its daily uploads in January 2025 to above 50% in June 2026, though it did not report their share of listening. In an experiment, access to AI story ideas made stories more creative on average but more similar to one another. Weekly use of AI chatbots for news rose from 7% to 10% of respondents worldwide in a year, with 16% of under-35s, while only 20% trusted the answers. Rights are the open question: the US Copyright Office has concluded that prompts alone do not make a user the author of the output, and music labels have moved from lawsuits to licensing deals with AI music services. We expect AI to be a normal tool in production and distribution by 2028, licensing arrangements to settle the main rights disputes in 2029–2032, and the question of what audiences will pay for to be the open one after that. Originality. The article sets the sector with the second-highest AI use in the EU beside experimental evidence on the limits of AI creativity, an audience survey and a company's upload data, and treats rights and transparency rules as part of the outlook, not as a footnote.

publications.title: Interpretable Cutting Plane Selection for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Using Genetic Programming
publications.abstract: Cutting planes (cuts) remove fractional solutions from mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) without excluding any feasible integer solutions, making them a key ingredient in modern MILP solvers. Current state-of-the-art solvers rely on fine-tuned handcrafted cut strategies, which, despite their effectiveness, remain inherently static and can be suboptimal. More recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to design adaptive cut strategies; however, most of these methods are based on neural networks, offering limited interpretability and providing no guarantees of convergence. In this paper, we propose \emph{Genetic Programming and Statistics-based Cut Selection} (GPSCS), the first learning-based framework that explicitly generalizes handcrafted cut selection heuristics into a fully interpretable policy. First, a genetic programming model evolves a symbolic scoring function that ranks candidate cuts using features derived from the cuts and the solving context. Second, a lightweight statistics-based mechanism adaptively determines the number of top-ranked cuts to add at each separation round by detecting significant score dropouts. We evaluate GPSCS within the SCIP solver on seven classes of synthetic and real-world benchmark instances, with a strong emphasis on generalization: evaluation instances are on average 41 times harder than those used for training. Experimental results show that GPSCS improves average solving time by $6\%$ compared to SCIP's default cut selection strategy and achieves a two-fold speedup over both a recent neural-network-based approach and a no-cut baseline, demonstrating strong robustness and generalization across heterogeneous MILP families.

publications.title: An experimental evaluation of static k-center clustering algorithms on graphs
publications.abstract: The $k$-center problem is one of the most fundamental clustering problems and has applications in a wide range of areas, including facility location, network design, data mining, and machine learning. Given a set of objects together with a distance measure, the goal is to select $k$ centers such that the maximum distance from any object to its closest center is minimized. The $k$-center problem has been studied extensively from a theoretical perspective, both in metric spaces and on graphs. While there have been experimental studies for $k$-center clustering in metric spaces, a comprehensive experimental comparison of graph-based $k$-center algorithms on large-scale graphs is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge this gap by evaluating a set of algorithms ranging from classical approaches such as Gonzalez's greedy algorithm [TCS 1985], an algorithm based on the framework established by Hochbaum and Shmoys [Math. Oper. Res. 1985], to more recent methods, including algorithms by Thorup [SICOMP 2001] and Abboud et al. [SOSA 2023]. Our study considers both running time, solution quality and the effects of parallelism on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art $k$-center algorithms on graphs and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches in practice.

publications.title: Guarding the Clinical Narrative: A Practitioner-Contributor's Retrospective Analysis of Open-Source Contributions to Clinical Natural Language Processing and Health-Data De-identification (2025-2026)
publications.abstract: Background. Clinical natural language processing (NLP) software extracts structured facts from free-text notes. De-identification software removes protected health information (PHI) so that text can be shared for research. A missed name or a broken date pattern can expose a patient or corrupt a dataset. Much of this software is open source, and outside contributors write part of it. Purpose. This study describes what one practitioner-contributor did in this area, what got merged, what did not, and what the review process taught about working well with maintainers. Methods. The data source was the author's public pull request (PR) record on GitHub, extracted with the GitHub REST API on 21 October 2026 (search: author:rtmalikian, type:pr). The full record held 213 PRs across 94 repositories. This paper analyses the clinical NLP and de-identification subset: 15 PRs in 5 repositories. Each PR was classed as merged, open, or closed unmerged. Seven cases were selected for close reading for their privacy or language point, or for a hard review lesson. Results. Eight of the 15 subset PRs merged, which is 61.5% of the 13 resolved PRs. Five closed unmerged. Two remained open. Merged work included a fix for placeholder collisions in a de-identification function, Italian and Spanish PHI locale packs, a date-pattern fix in a French hospital NLP library, and a change that stopped PHI entering version control. The hardest case, a Spanish locale pack, survived a blocking review that found real damage in a follow-up commit. A fix-forward commit repaired it, and the PR merged the next day. Conclusions. The record points to a plain finding. PHI safety in this software rests on ordinary engineering habits: reproduction before repair, small scope, tests run before submission, and calm correction when a reviewer finds a fault. Language coverage is part of safety. De-identification that works only in English leaves other patients less protected.

publications.title: Supplementary material for 'Two commons without shared references: Bibliographic coupling between library resource-sharing and research-data interoperability literatures, 2000 to 2025'
publications.abstract: Supplementary material for a manuscript under double-anonymous peer review. Author information is withheld during review and will be added after the review process. The document reports the Scopus search strategy, the eligibility criteria and decision rules, the coding scheme for primary label and object, the predictions written down before the OpenAlex data were retrieved, the six unresolvable OpenAlex identifiers removed from the reference data, the test results including a post hoc sensitivity analysis, and the list of the 327 included papers with Scopus EID, DOI, codes and OpenAlex work identifier. Scopus records themselves are not redistributed.

publications.title: DCM Artefact Governance: research-software and artefact archive
publications.abstract: Research-software and artefact archive accompanying the DCM Artefact Governance paper, An Artefact-Level Governance Pattern for Model Outputs Under Deep Uncertainty, which is in preparation for Environmental Modelling & Software. The manuscript is not included. The archive contains IncrementalElectricityPack and BiomassSupplyPack schemas, governed artefacts, hourly incremental-electricity traces, future-specific multipliers, validators, fixtures, screening calculations and figure scripts. The single command python reproduce.py re-executes the documented checks and calculations and regenerates Figure 2 from the supplied inputs. The archive does not regenerate the upstream process-heat dispatch model run or the future-specific multipliers, and passing the checks does not validate the underlying models or the third-party source estimates. Licensing. The licence field of this record shows MIT because a Zenodo record holds a single licence identifier. The archive's licensing is set by the licence files it contains, which remain authoritative: source code, JSON Schemas, test fixtures and build configuration are licensed under MIT (LICENSE); original project data, figures and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA.md); values reproduced from Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) (2022), Regional Energy Transition Accelerator (RETA): Southland – Phase One Report, are third-party material excluded from both licences and remain subject to their source's terms (see LICENSE-DATA.md, DATA_SOURCES.md and EECA_CONTENT_INVENTORY.csv).

publications.title: Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: code, derived data and results.
publications.abstract: Companion deposit of the manuscript "Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: A Functional Taxonomy and a Test of Text-Based Risk Metrics Under Context Truncation of Clinical Text", submitted to the Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments. The deposit contains the code, derived data and results behind every number, table and figure of the manuscript: the three cohorts of 43 instances (ACI-Bench, MedQA, PMC-Patients) under complete context, partial and severe truncation; the 645 generated alerts; the per-alert metric values, including the model-reference agreement metric computed as defined by Equation (3); the anonymous ratings of 86 alerts by two physicians, with the blind design and its key; the analysis scripts and their recorded outputs; and the IEEE Xplore search evidence. Every analysis script was run again from this deposit before submission and reproduces its recorded output. The README maps each item of the manuscript to its input files, script and output. Third-party excerpts keep the licences of their sources, listed in the README.

publications.title: CatCraft Anti-Cheat A1: A Server-Side Multi-Signal Corroboration Anti-Cheat System for Counter-Strike 2 (Technical Report)
publications.abstract: Cheat detection in first-person shooter (FPS) games has long relied on client-side anti-cheat and black-box machine-learning models, while dedicated servers are often reduced to replay storage and manual review. This report presents CatCraft Anti-Cheat A1 (v0.6.0-b7, CCAC-A1), a server-side multi-signal corroboration anti-cheat system deployed on a Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) dedicated server. The data plane combines an engine ProcessUsercmds hook, server-side entity ground truth, game events, client cvars, and network statistics, and implements 19 detection modules with 25 independent judges (plus one aim sub-judge). Three engineering mechanisms are proposed: (1) three-tier punishment with sub-module corroboration, where a conjunction judge may only escalate to a permanent ban when all bound sub-modules confirm; (2) kinematic corroboration using event-window vs player-baseline variance, plus an input-output causal consistency sub-judge based on mousedx/mousedy; and (3) stability-first online protection against client message flooding. The system has been running on a live community server in DryRun mode, backed by a MySQL evidence store and per-map SourceTV demos. We report the design, observed judge behaviour, false-positive corrections, and limitations. This is a technical report based on preliminary deployment experience on a single server; it is not a controlled experiment and makes no claim about detection or false-positive rates. This record contains the English technical report (primary) and the Chinese original (additional file). It is not a peer-reviewed publication.
